title: Quantum-enabled active matter at the atomic scale
authors: Sabrina Burgardt, Julian Feß, Alexander Guthmann, Silvia Hiebel, Aritra K. Mukhopadhyay, Sangyun Lee, Michael te Vrugt, Benno Liebchen, Hartmut Löwen, Raphael Wittkowski, Artur Widera
abstract: Active matter comprises particles that extract energy from their local environment and convert it into motion. Although active particles have been miniaturized down to the nanoscale, realizing activity at the fundamentally smaller scale of individual atoms remains an open challenge, where quantum effects become increasingly relevant. Here, we experimentally demonstrate that individual Cs-133 atoms confined in an optical dipole trap extract energy from an ultracold bath of Rb-87 atoms via quantum-mechanical spin interactions and convert it into active motion. We quantitatively reproduce the resulting dynamics using a parameter-free active Langevin model derived from kinetic theory and support it with event-driven Monte Carlo collision simulations. The microscopic origin of activity is identified as quantum spin exchange, which transfers discrete internal spin energy into kinetic motion. Our work establishes a quantum-enabled route to active matter at the fundamental size limit of single atoms and opens perspectives for exploring the interplay of activity, quantum physics, and mesoscopic non-equilibrium thermodynamics.
summary: The research experimentally demonstrates how single Cs atoms can become 'active' particles by harvesting energy from their surrounding Rb bath through inelastic quantum spin-exchange collisions. By coupling the discrete quantum spin dynamics to continuous motional motion, they develop and validate an active Langevin model that successfully predicts the transient broadening of the atomic density distribution. This work opens a novel platform for studying non-equilibrium thermodynamics at the fundamental single-atom scale.
main_problem: The primary challenge is realizing active matter at the fundamental atomic scale where quantum mechanical effects govern energy transfer, moving beyond classical descriptions.
main_result: The authors experimentally demonstrate that individual Cs atoms can achieve directed, active motion by extracting internal spin energy from a surrounding Rb bath via inelastic quantum spin-exchange collisions. This establishes a quantum-enabled route to single-atom active matter.
method: The work combines experimental measurements of atomic density distributions with theoretical modeling using parameter-free active Langevin equations and event-driven Monte Carlo simulations derived from kinetic theory.
model_or_system: The system consists of individual Cs atoms confined in an optical dipole trap immersed in a thermal bath of Rb atoms. Activity is driven by inelastic s-wave spin-exchange collisions, which convert discrete internal spin energy into measurable kinetic motion.
key_observables: Cs density distribution width (s_{z,Cs}), time delay of peak broadening, and the magnitude of the active force/energy injection ($Q$).
important_parameters: Magnetic field strength (B), collision energy relative to activation energy ($E_c$ vs $Q$), and temperature of the bath ($	ext{T}_{	ext{Rb}}$).
main_assumptions: The Rb cloud is treated as a Markovian bath, and the activity mechanism relies on breaking detailed balance via non-reciprocal spin exchange rates.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the quantum mechanism (Fig. 1) showing energy transfer from spin to motion; later figures show density broadening measurements ($s_{z,	ext{Cs}}$) as a function of time and magnetic field, comparing theory/simulation to experiment.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the physical system and quantum mechanism (spin-exchange), deriving the necessary theoretical framework (Langevin model from kinetic theory), presenting experimental measurements of activity signatures (density broadening), and finally validating the model against varying external parameters like magnetic field strength.
why_interesting: This work sits at the intersection of AMO physics, non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, and quantum dynamics. The ability to engineer directed motion using internal quantum degrees of freedom in ultracold atoms is a major step toward quantum simulation of active matter.

Spin-momentum entanglement.note: The experimental demonstration of directed motion (momentum) arising directly from inelastic quantum spin-exchange collisions establishes a clear mechanism for coupling internal spin energy to external motional degrees of freedom, which is the core concept of spin-momentum entanglement.
